title: The respiratory system
note: Air moves along pressure gradients: contracting the diaphragm enlarges the thorax and lowers alveolar pressure below atmospheric (Boyle's law). Each gas then diffuses down its own partial-pressure gradient. Nearly all O2 travels bound to hemoglobin, and most CO2 travels as bicarbonate made by carbonic anhydrase in red cells.

read.title: Down the pressure gradient
text: Air flows into the lungs for the same reason it rushes out of a squeezed balloon: gases move from higher pressure to lower. When the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the external intercostals lift the ribs, the thoracic cavity enlarges. By Boyle's law, the larger volume lowers the pressure in the alveoli below atmospheric pressure, and air flows in. Quiet exhalation is mostly passive: the muscles relax, elastic tissue recoils, alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric, and air flows out.

Once air reaches the alveoli, each gas moves along its own partial-pressure gradient. Alveolar oxygen sits near 104 mm Hg, while blood returning from the tissues arrives at about 40, so oxygen diffuses across the thin respiratory membrane into the blood. Carbon dioxide moves the other way, from about 45 mm Hg in the blood to about 40 in the alveoli. That gradient is small, but carbon dioxide is about twenty times more soluble than oxygen, so similar amounts of the two gases cross.

In the tissues the gradients reverse. Active cells use oxygen and produce carbon dioxide, so oxygen leaves the blood and carbon dioxide enters it. Nearly all the oxygen travels bound to hemoglobin, and most of the carbon dioxide is converted to bicarbonate inside red blood cells.
